claims.text: Phase stability in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloys is governed by the degree of short-range chemical ordering.
High-temperature strength, environmental resistance, radiation tolerance, and cryogenic toughness in these alloys are governed by short-range chemical ordering.
Controlled annealing can modestly enhance short-range chemical ordering and form nanoscale Al-rich ordered clusters.
The Al-rich ordered clusters adopt B2 or L12 arrangements within an FCC matrix.
Enhanced short-range order reduces atomic mobility and elemental diffusion.
Enhanced short-range order impedes coarsening of secondary phases.
Finely dispersed ordered clusters act as sinks for irradiation-induced defects.
Short-range order and ordered clusters enhance dislocation pinning.
Enhanced dislocation pinning increases high-temperature yield strength while maintaining ductility.
Modest short-range ordering stabilizes the FCC matrix.
Finely dispersed ordered clusters act as barriers to corrosion.
Finely dispersed ordered clusters do not impair cryogenic toughness.
Tuned short-range order inhibits crack propagation and thereby maintains or improves cryogenic toughness relative to the rapidly quenched baseline.
Tuned short-range order improves corrosion resistance relative to the rapidly quenched baseline.
Tuned short-range order improves radiation tolerance by reducing irradiation-induced defect accumulation relative to the rapidly quenched baseline.
A rapidly quenched baseline has minimal short-range ordering.
Annealing at 700°C for progressively longer times from 1 to 20 hours progressively promotes short-range order and nanoscale Al-rich cluster formation.
Beyond a critical ordering level, further annealing or transition to long-range order degrades the targeted properties.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis predicts that excessive annealing and long-range order reverse the benefits, while the boundary says conditions producing long-range order fall outside the hypothesis's scope.

The hypothesis itself predicts underperformance after ordering exceeds a critical level, but the falsification rule states broadly that samples with higher SRO that underperform the baseline would falsify the mechanism. Underperformance at high ordering levels could instead agree with the proposed nonmonotonic response.
